text: I often say to find your audience's cultural erogenous zones. So what it means is people have things that they either care about or don't, and you're not going to change that.
speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
context: Lenny asks Lulu about what helps an idea spread effectively. Lulu introduces her framework of finding your audience's 'cultural erogenous zones' - the topics and values that naturally excite and engage specific groups of people. She explains that rather than trying to change people's existing passions or worldviews (which requires enormous effort), it's much more effective to adapt your message to align with what they already care deeply about.
text_ko: 저는 자주 청중의 문화적 민감 지점(cultural erogenous zones)을 찾아보라고 말해요. 그 말은 사람들이 어떤 것에는 관심을 갖고 어떤 것에는 전혀 관심이 없다는 거고, 그건 바꿀 수 없다는 뜻이에요.
text_zh: 我常说，要找到你受众的文化敏感点(cultural erogenous zones)。意思是人们对某些事很在乎，对另一些事毫不关心，而你改变不了这一点。
text_es: Yo suelo decir que hay que identificar los puntos sensibles culturales (cultural erogenous zones) de tu audiencia. Eso significa que hay temas que a la gente le importan y otros que no, y no vas a poder cambiar eso.
key_sentence: Find your audience's cultural erogenous zones to shape your message effectively.
original_text: I often say to find your audience's cultural erogenous zones. So what it means is people have things that they either care about or don't, and you're not going to change that. So it's a huge lift to try to change someone's worldview or their passions. It's a light lift to take the thing you want to talk about and just shape it into, to fit into their worldview or their passions.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to the ideas, customs, and social behavior of a particular people or society.
vocabulary.businessContext: Understanding cultural aspects is vital for businesses operating in diverse markets, as it influences consumer behavior and marketing strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'cultural' often carries a connotation of depth and complexity, suggesting that it encompasses more than just surface-level traits.

vocabulary.definition: A group of people who are intended to receive or engage with a particular message or content.
vocabulary.businessContext: Identifying and understanding the target audience is essential for effective marketing, product development, and communication strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'audience' can imply a passive group, but in modern contexts, it often suggests an interactive relationship with the content provider.

text: You have to make it memorable and you have to make people want to say it of their own volition. And so what doesn't make them want to say it is doing a favor for a corporation.
speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
context: Lenny asks Lulu broadly what she's learned about what helps an idea spread. Lulu explains the fundamental principle that ideas spread when people are intrinsically motivated to repeat them, not when they feel like they're doing a favor for a company. She identifies the key motivations that drive people to share content: bringing joy to others, making people laugh, appearing interesting, or expressing their identity.
text_ko: 기억에 남게 만들어야 하고, 사람들이 스스로 말하고 싶게 만들어야 해요. 그런데 기업을 위해 호의를 베푸는 것처럼 느껴지면 사람들은 말하려 하지 않아요.
text_zh: 你得让它朗朗上口，让人愿意自发地说出来。不会让人自发说的，往往就是那种明显在替公司打广告的东西。
text_es: Hay que hacerlo memorable y lograr que la gente quiera decirlo por iniciativa propia. Lo que no les da ganas de decirlo es que parezca que están haciendo un favor a una empresa.
key_sentence: Make people want to say it of their own volition, not just for a corporation.
original_text: You have to make it memorable and you have to make people want to say it of their own volition. And so what doesn't make them want to say it is doing a favor for a corporation. What does make them want to say it is they want to bring joy to somebody else, they want to make somebody laugh, they want to appear interesting, or they want to project some part of their identity.

vocabulary.definition: Easily remembered or recalled; having qualities that make it significant or noteworthy.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, creating memorable branding or marketing campaigns is crucial for customer retention and brand loyalty.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'memorable' often has a positive connotation, it can also imply that something is overly flashy or gimmicky if not executed well.

vocabulary.definition: The power of using one's will to make decisions or take actions; the act of choosing or deciding.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate setting, understanding employee volition is essential for fostering a motivated workforce and encouraging initiative.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'volition' often carries a formal tone and is typically used in discussions about autonomy and decision-making processes.

text: I think if you're a startup your enemy is the status quo. And when you don't take risks, when you minimize risk by doing nothing, the best way to minimize risk is to do nothing. You're letting the status quo win.
speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
context: Lenny asks Lulu about her philosophy of taking risks as a communications person, noting that many comms professionals tend to be very conservative. Lulu explains why startups in particular must take risks in their communications strategy. She argues that for startups, avoiding risk by doing nothing actually allows their biggest competitor - the status quo - to win without any challenge.
text_ko: 제 생각에는 스타트업(startup)이라면 가장 큰 적은 바로 현상 유지(status quo)예요. 위험(risk)을 감수하지 않고 아무것도 안 하면서 위험을 줄이려 하면, 결국 현상 유지가 이기도록 만드는 거예요.
text_zh: 我觉得，创业公司最大的敌人就是现状（status quo）。如果你不敢冒险，想通过什么都不做来把风险降到最低——毕竟把风险降到最低最直接的办法就是不行动——那你就是在把主动权拱手让给现状。
text_es: Creo que si eres una startup, tu enemigo es el status quo. Y cuando no tomas riesgos —cuando intentas minimizar el riesgo no haciendo nada— la mejor manera de minimizarlo es no hacer nada; así estás dejando que el status quo gane.
key_sentence: Minimizing risk by doing nothing lets the status quo win by default.
original_text: I think if you're a startup your enemy is the status quo. And when you don't take risks, when you minimize risk by doing nothing, the best way to minimize risk is to do nothing. You're letting the status quo win. You're letting your greatest enemy and rival and threat to your business win by default, because you're not even going to try to compete.

vocabulary.definition: The existing state of affairs or current condition in a particular context.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, the status quo often refers to established practices, norms, or market conditions that companies may seek to challenge or change.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often carries a negative connotation in innovative contexts, suggesting stagnation or resistance to change.

vocabulary.definition: To reduce the potential for loss or negative outcomes in a given situation.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups, minimizing risk is crucial for decision-making, often involving strategies to avoid financial loss or operational failures.
vocabulary.nuance: While minimizing risk is generally seen as prudent, excessive caution can hinder innovation and growth.

vocabulary.definition: To engage in actions that involve exposure to danger or loss in pursuit of a desired outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: Taking risks is often essential for startups aiming for growth, innovation, and competitive advantage in dynamic markets.
vocabulary.nuance: The phrase suggests a willingness to step outside comfort zones, but it should be balanced with calculated decision-making.

text: If your natural audience cares about X and you're offering Y, then it's your job to create the API or to create the bridge from X to Y. With messaging, it's not build it and they will come.
speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
context: Lenny asks Lulu to elaborate on her 'cultural erogenous zones' framework and wants examples of it in action. Lulu explains that when there's a mismatch between what your audience cares about and what you're offering, your job is to create connections between them. She emphasizes that the 'build it and they will come' approach rarely works in messaging - it's extremely difficult to create content so compelling that it changes someone's fundamental interests.
text_ko: 만약 당신의 자연스러운 청중이 X에 관심이 있고 당신이 Y를 제공하고 있다면, X에서 Y로 연결해 주는 API(응용 프로그램 인터페이스)나 다리를 만드는 건 당신 일이에요. 메시징(messaging)은 ‘만들어 놓으면 사람들이 올 거다’처럼 되는 게 아니에요.
text_zh: 如果你的目标受众关心 X，而你提供的是 Y，那你的工作就是把 X 和 Y 连起来——要么做个接口(API)，要么搭座桥把两者连接起来。至于信息传达(messaging)，别指望“建好了他们就会来”。
text_es: Si a tu audiencia natural le importa X y tú ofreces Y, tienes que crear la interfaz de programación (API) o construir el puente entre X y Y. En materia de mensajería (messaging), no basta con construirlo y esperar que vengan.
key_sentence: Create the API to connect your audience's interests with your offerings.
original_text: If your natural audience cares about X and you're offering Y, then it's your job to create the API or to create the bridge from X to Y. With messaging, it's not build it and they will come. It is so hard and you'd have to be superhumanly gifted to the extent that I can't recall seeing in my entire life, where you create a message and a story so powerful that someone who didn't care at all before suddenly makes that their passion.

vocabulary.definition: To establish a connection or pathway between two distinct elements, concepts, or groups.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, 'creating the bridge' often refers to developing solutions that connect customer needs with product offerings, facilitating better communication and understanding.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase implies an active role in problem-solving and innovation, suggesting that one must take initiative rather than waiting for solutions to emerge.

vocabulary.definition: The process of conveying information, ideas, or values through various forms of communication.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, 'messaging' refers to how a company communicates its brand, products, and values to its target audience, often through marketing strategies and public relations.
vocabulary.nuance: Effective messaging is crucial for engagement and persuasion, and it should be tailored to resonate with the specific audience being addressed.

vocabulary.definition: A group of individuals who receive or engage with a particular message or content.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and communications, understanding the 'audience' is critical for tailoring messages and campaigns to effectively reach and influence potential customers.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a specific demographic or psychographic segment, highlighting the importance of targeted communication strategies.

text: First, you have to acknowledge that you're the underdog, and you're not going to use the GE playbook from the 1980s or whatever.
speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
context: Lenny asks what works best for underdog startups and companies trying to get attention against incumbent competitors. Lulu explains that underdog companies must first acknowledge their position and avoid trying to use the same strategies that work for established corporations with vast resources. She emphasizes that underdogs can't rely on having extensive resources, deep industry relationships, institutional support, or the ability to benefit from existing market narratives.
text_ko: 먼저 자신이 언더독(underdog)이라는 걸 인정해야 해요. 그리고 1980년대 GE식 플레이북(playbook)을 그대로 가져다 쓰진 않을 거예요.
text_zh: 先得承认你处于劣势，别指望还能照搬80年代GE那套玩法（GE playbook）什么的。
text_es: Primero tienes que reconocer que eres el que parte en desventaja (underdog), y que no vas a seguir el manual de GE (playbook) de los años 80 ni nada por el estilo.
key_sentence: Acknowledge being the underdog and avoid the GE playbook from the 1980s.
original_text: First, you have to acknowledge that you're the underdog, and you're not going to use the GE playbook from the 1980s or whatever. So acknowledging that means knowing that you're not going to play the game that requires you to have more resources, more and deeper relationships, and institutional backings, and to be able to draft off of the current narrative.

vocabulary.definition: To recognize the existence, validity, or truth of something.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, acknowledging a challenge or a competitor's strengths is crucial for strategic planning and decision-making.
vocabulary.nuance: While it implies acceptance, it can also suggest a proactive approach to addressing issues rather than ignoring them.

vocabulary.definition: A set of strategies or guidelines used to achieve specific objectives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and tech, a playbook serves as a reference for best practices and operational procedures, often tailored to the unique needs of the organization.
vocabulary.nuance: While it suggests a structured approach, it can also imply rigidity if not adapted to changing circumstances.

vocabulary.definition: A competitor thought to have little chance of winning or succeeding.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, underdogs often represent startups or smaller companies that challenge larger, established firms, appealing to consumers' support for the 'little guy.'
vocabulary.nuance: The term can evoke sympathy and support, but may also suggest a lack of resources or experience compared to competitors.

text: So you take out your one-page Google Doc. I feel like most comms problems can be solved with one-page Google Doc.
speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
context: Lenny asks Lulu for practical advice on how someone should implement her concentric circles framework for spreading messages to different audience groups. Lulu provides a tactical approach, suggesting people create a simple one-page document to map out their target audiences. She emphasizes keeping it manageable by limiting to five or six audience groups, noting that having more audiences than that indicates the company has moved beyond early-stage challenges.
text_ko: 그럼 한 페이지짜리 구글 문서(Google Doc)를 꺼내 보세요. 대부분의 소통 문제는 그 한 장으로 해결되는 것 같아요.
text_zh: 你把那份一页的 Google 文档 (Google Doc) 拿出来。我觉得大多数沟通问题，一页文档就能解决。
text_es: Así que sacas tu documento de una página (Google Doc). Me parece que la mayoría de los problemas de comunicación (comms) se resuelven con algo así.
key_sentence: Most comms problems can be solved with a one-page Google Doc, not a first world problem.
original_text: So you take out your one-page Google Doc. I feel like most comms problems can be solved with one-page Google Doc. So you go to your one-page Google Doc and you take your audiences, you list them, probably stop at five or six because past that it's like way, way first world problem.

text: LinkedIn is super underutilized because it gets a ton of eyeballs in time, but most of the content sucks. 95% of the content this is not scientific - this is my might estimate.
speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
context: Lenny mentions that he gets more newsletter traffic from LinkedIn than Twitter and asks Lulu for her perspective on this platform choice. Lulu explains why LinkedIn represents an underutilized opportunity for professionals and founders. She argues that while LinkedIn receives significant user attention and engagement, the vast majority of content is low-quality social pleasantries rather than genuinely valuable information, creating an opportunity for those who post substantial content.
text_ko: LinkedIn은 정말 활용도가 낮아요. 사람들이 많이 보긴 하는데 대부분의 콘텐츠가 형편없어서 제대로 활용되지 않고 있어요. 제 대략적인 추정으로는 그중 95%는 과학적 근거가 없어요.
text_zh: 领英（LinkedIn）没被好好利用，明明能带来大量曝光，但大部分内容质量很差。我估计大概95%的内容都是这样——这不是科学结论，只是我的粗略估计。
text_es: LinkedIn está muy infrautilizado: consigue muchísima visibilidad con el tiempo, pero el problema es que la mayor parte del contenido es de baja calidad. Diría que el 95% de ese contenido no está basado en evidencia científica —es una estimación mía—.
key_sentence: LinkedIn is super underutilized despite having a ton of eyeballs.
original_text: LinkedIn is super underutilized because it gets a ton of eyeballs in time, but most of the content sucks. 95% of the content this is not scientific - this is my might estimate. 95% of the content is people congratulating each other on work anniversaries or people saying, 'I'm so proud of my team for this thing they did.'

vocabulary.definition: Not being used to its full potential or capacity.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, an underutilized resource, such as a platform or tool, indicates that there is significant untapped value that could be harnessed for greater efficiency or effectiveness.
vocabulary.nuance: This term often carries a negative connotation, suggesting that opportunities are being missed due to lack of engagement or investment.

vocabulary.definition: Information or material created and shared for communication, marketing, or educational purposes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of digital marketing and social media, high-quality content is crucial for engaging audiences and driving brand awareness.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply varying levels of quality; 'content' alone may suggest a neutral or low-quality standard unless specified otherwise.

vocabulary.definition: An approximate calculation or judgment regarding the value, number, quantity, or extent of something.
vocabulary.businessContext: Estimates are commonly used in project management and financial forecasting to provide a basis for decision-making and resource allocation.
vocabulary.nuance: While estimates are inherently uncertain, they should be based on informed assumptions to maintain credibility.
